questions.question: What is the this keyword in Java and what are its uses?
questions.title: this Keyword in Java — All Uses
questions.direct_answer: `this` is a reference to the **current object** inside an instance method or constructor. Its main uses are: disambiguating instance fields from parameters (`this.name = name`), calling another constructor in the same class (`this()`), and passing the current object as an argument.

interviewer_intent.testing: Complete knowledge of all uses of this — disambiguation, constructor chaining, and passing self
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking this is only for disambiguation — missing the constructor chaining and self-passing uses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that this cannot be used in static methods — there's no object context in a static method

sections.title: Three Uses of this
Key Points
sections.content:
- `this.field` — disambiguate instance field from local variable/parameter with same name
- `this()` — constructor chaining within the same class (must be first statement)
- `this` as argument — pass current object to another method
- `return this` — enables method chaining (builder pattern, fluent API)
- `this` is NOT available in `static` methods — no object context
- `this` refers to the runtime object, not the declared type
- Common interview question: `this` in a constructor of a subclass refers to the subclass object, not the parent

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The `this` keyword refers to the current object inside an instance method or constructor. It has four main uses: first, disambiguating a field from a parameter when they have the same name — `this.name = name`. Second, calling another constructor in the same class using `this()` — must be the first statement. Third, passing the current object to another method as an argument. Fourth, returning `this` from a method to enable method chaining in builder patterns. The key constraint is that `this` can only be used in instance context — not in static methods where there's no associated object.

questions.question: What is the super keyword in Java and when do you need it?
questions.title: super Keyword in Java — Uses and Rules
questions.direct_answer: `super` refers to the **parent class** of the current object. It is used in three ways: `super()` to call the parent constructor, `super.method()` to call an overridden parent method, and `super.field` to access a parent field hidden by a child field with the same name.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all three uses and the constraint that super() must be the first statement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking super.field is needed often — field hiding is rare in practice; the more important uses are super() and super.method()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that super.method() is essential when you want to extend parent behavior — logging, permission checks, calling parent logic then adding more

sections.title: Three Uses of super
Key Points
sections.content:
- `super()` — call parent constructor; MUST be the first statement in constructor
- `super.method()` — call the parent's version of an overridden instance method
- `super.field` — access a parent field hidden by a child field with the same name
- Cannot be used in `static` methods (no object context)
- `super` always refers to the direct parent, not a grandparent or further ancestor
- Cannot be stored in a variable or passed as a reference
- `super.method()` only works one level up — `super.super.method()` is NOT valid

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The `super` keyword refers to the parent class. It has three uses: `super()` calls the parent's constructor and must be the first line in a constructor; `super.method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method — useful when you want to extend rather than replace the parent's behavior; and `super.field` accesses a parent field that's been hidden by a child field of the same name. `super` can only be used in instance context, not in static methods, and it always refers to the direct parent — you can't chain it like `super.super`.

questions.question: Why can't you have both this() and super() in the same constructor?
questions.title: this() and super() Cannot Coexist in Same Constructor
questions.direct_answer: Both `this()` and `super()` must be the **first statement** in a constructor, and there can only be one first statement. You cannot use both in the same constructor. The compiler enforces this, resulting in a compile error if you try.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the first-statement rule and why it's a hard constraint
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you can call both to chain to a sibling constructor AND call the parent — structurally impossible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how the constraint is resolved: the delegated-to sibling constructor is responsible for calling super() if needed

sections.title: The Single First Statement Constraint
Key Points
sections.content:
- Both `this()` and `super()` must be the first statement — only one can be first
- Putting both in the same constructor = compile error
- Resolution: the constructor using `this()` delegates; the delegated constructor calls `super()`
- The parent constructor WILL eventually be called through the chain
- If neither `this()` nor `super()` is written, Java inserts `super()` automatically
- This is why constructor chaining always terminates at a `super()` call
- Ensures the full parent hierarchy is initialized in every code path

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You can't have both `this()` and `super()` in the same constructor because both must be the first statement, and there can only be one first statement. If you try, the compiler gives an error. The way to handle this is through delegation: the constructor that uses `this()` delegates to a sibling constructor, and that sibling constructor is responsible for calling `super()`. So the parent still gets initialized — just through the chain rather than directly. Every constructor chain eventually reaches a `super()` call, ensuring the parent hierarchy is always initialized.

questions.question: What happens when a subclass instance method calls this.method() where method() is overridden?
questions.title: this.method() Call in Context of Overriding
questions.direct_answer: When you call `this.method()` inside a subclass, the **actual runtime type** of the object determines which version of `method()` executes. If the current object is of a subclass that has overridden `method()`, the subclass version runs — even if `this.method()` is called from a parent class method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of dynamic dispatch and that this in a parent method still dispatches to the subclass override
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking a parent method calling this.method() will always call the parent's version — it calls the most-derived version
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the implication for the Template Method pattern and note the gotcha: calling overridable methods from constructors can be dangerous

sections.title: this Always Dispatches Dynamically
Key Points
sections.content:
- `this.method()` always uses dynamic dispatch — the most-derived override runs
- This enables the Template Method pattern: parent defines algorithm, child fills in steps
- Dangerous: calling overridable methods from constructors can see uninitialized subclass state
- The subclass fields are not initialized when the parent constructor runs
- Best practice: never call overridable (non-final, non-private) methods from constructors
- To avoid dynamic dispatch, make the method `final` or `private`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When `this.method()` is called, it always uses dynamic dispatch — the most derived version of the method runs based on the actual object type. So if a Parent method calls `this.setup()` and the actual object is a Child with an overridden `setup()`, Child's version runs. This is the foundation of the Template Method pattern. The important gotcha is that calling overridable methods from constructors is dangerous — when the Parent constructor runs, the Child's fields haven't been initialized yet, so the Child's override might see uninitialized state. That's why constructors should avoid calling methods that subclasses can override.

followup_questions: Why is it dangerous to call overridable methods from a constructor?
How do final methods prevent the dynamic dispatch issue in constructors?

questions.question: Can you use this or super in a static method in Java?
questions.title: this and super in Static Methods — Java Rules
questions.direct_answer: **No.** Both `this` and `super` cannot be used in `static` methods. `this` refers to the current object instance, and `super` refers to the parent object — but static methods belong to the **class**, not any specific instance. There is no object context in a static method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the fundamental difference between static (class-level) and instance (object-level) context
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to use this in a static method and not understanding why it's a compile error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the logical reason: this is a reference to an object, static methods can run without any object being created — so there's nothing for this to refer to

sections.title: No Object Context in Static Methods
Key Points
sections.content:
- Static methods belong to the class, not to any object
- `this` requires an object context — static methods have none
- `super` also requires an object context — not available in static
- Using `this` or `super` in a static method = **compile error**
- Static methods can access only static fields and call only static methods directly
- Instance methods can access both instance AND static members (they have an object context)
- `main()` is static — that's why you can't access instance members directly in `main()`

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: No, you can't use `this` or `super` in a static method, and the reason is logical. Static methods belong to the class, not to any specific object — you can call them without ever creating an instance. So when a static method runs, there's no object, and `this` has nothing to refer to. The same applies to `super`. Using either in a static method gives a compile error: 'non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context.' Static methods can only directly access other static members.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using super.method() when overriding a method?
questions.title: Using super.method() to Extend Parent Behavior
questions.direct_answer: Calling `super.method()` inside an overriding method invokes the **parent's original implementation** before or after adding new behavior. This allows you to **extend** the parent's behavior rather than completely replacing it — a common pattern in frameworks like Android, Spring, and the Template Method pattern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the practical use of super.method() for extending behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always completely replacing the parent method without calling super — losing important parent behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how frameworks require super calls: Android's Activity lifecycle, Spring's filter chains, JPA's equals/hashCode

sections.title: Extending vs Replacing Parent Behavior
Key Points
sections.content:
- `super.method()` calls the parent's version inside the child's override
- Can call before the new code (setup), after (cleanup), or both (wrapping)
- Many frameworks REQUIRE calling `super.method()` — skipping it causes bugs or exceptions
- Without `super.method()`, you're completely replacing the parent's behavior
- Commonly required: Android lifecycle methods, JUnit setUp/tearDown, Spring MVC methods
- `super.method()` can appear anywhere in the method body (unlike `super()` in constructors)
- Not required — it's the developer's choice — but often semantically necessary

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When you override a method and call `super.method()`, you're keeping the parent's logic while adding your own. This extends rather than replaces the behavior. For example, I might override a `log()` method to add timestamps, calling `super.log()` to still do the original logging and then appending the time. In framework development this is very important — Android's `onCreate()` must call `super.onCreate()` or the app throws an exception because the framework needs the parent's initialization to run. The position of `super.method()` in your override depends on whether you want the parent logic to run before or after your additions.
